newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban Foreign Ministry seeks to play down row with Spain.
newsitem.headline: Cuban Foreign Ministry seeks to play down row with Spain.

text.p: The Cuban Foreign Ministry sought on Thursday to play down a dispute with Spain that has erupted over Cuban charges that Madrid is meddling in its affairs, saying Havana had made its move and was now waiting to see what would happen.

But a senior figure in the Cuban hierarchy kept up strong criticism of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's conservative government over Spanish calls for political reform in Cuba. Parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon, a member of the Communist Party Politburo, said some members of the Spanish administration were "racist and colonialist."

And the Communist Party daily Granma dedicated one of its eight pages on Thursday to an article attacking the recent setting up in Madrid of a foundation of Cuban exiles that aims to press for change in Cuba.

The foundation includes a member of Aznar's ruling Popular Party as well as a well-known hardline exile critic of President Fidel Castro, Jorge Mas Canosa. Its setting up, and Aznar's links with Mas Canosa, have infuriated Cuba.

Tensions between Havana and Madrid that have simmered for weeks boiled over on Tuesday when the Cuban Foreign Ministry protested angrily to the Spanish government and announced it was withdrawing official approval for a new Spanish ambassador.

However, Foreign Ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso said the ministry had noted that the Spanish government said that it was willing to treat the issue calmly, and that it did not want to esacalate the situation.
"From the point of view of the Cuban Foreign Ministry, the same willingness can be seen," he told a regular weekly news briefing.
Alfonso added the situation with Spain was now at a "certain level" and that since Cuba's move on Tuesday there had not been new elements to "worsen or improve it notably".
Havana had taken the step it viewed as necessary "and now we have to wait to see what happens... and it no longer depends on us," he said, adding "we are completely calm".

Alfonso was asked about Alarcon's less conciliatory comments, published earlier on Thursday by the Cuban state news agency AIN. Alfonso said he was not yet aware of these remarks and so was not prepared to comment.

Alarcon, speaking in the eastern city of Santiago de Cuba, said that "in this new (Spanish) administration it seems there are some people ...with a racist, colonialist mentality". But he added that most Spanish people and politicians, including many people in conservative ranks, had a reasonable and rational attitude towards Cuba.
"It's unacceptable that there are politicians who want to treat Cuba as though it were a slave nation," Alarcon said.

Asked about a new European Union plan to increase pressure for reform in Cuba, a re-drafted version of a Spanish initiative that is due to be approved next week by EU Foreign Ministers, Alfonso said the Cuban government preferred not to comment until it had full knowledge of the document and until it had been approved.
But in general, Cuba believed that normal relations between Cuba and other states "cannot be based on political preconditions", he said.
Apparently reflecting the Foreign Ministry's efforts to play down tensions, a huge security operation around the Spanish embassy in Havana aimed at heading off any incident was reduced on Thursday.
Although the embassy was still guarded by a several dozen police officers and members of civil order groups, they were far fewer than on previous days.
On Wednesday, hundreds of police and members of civilian order groups formed tight cordons around the embassy area, sealing off the streets surrounding the building.
